title: How the Printing Press Changed the World

scenes.narration: Imagine a world where every book had to be copied by hand. Before the 1440s in Europe, one scribe could spend [[months]] on a single book, so books were rare and expensive.
Then, in the German city of Mainz, a goldsmith named [[Johannes Gutenberg]] had an idea: a press with movable metal letters that could be reused again and again.
The press squeezed inked metal letters onto paper. Once the letters were set, he could print many identical pages, far faster than any scribe could write them.
Around 1455, his workshop produced the famous [[Gutenberg Bible]], one of the first major books printed in Europe with movable type.
Printed books were cheaper to make, so more people could afford them, and more people learned to read. Soon, presses were opening in cities across Europe.
Now ideas could spread far faster than ever before. Pamphlets and books carried new arguments from town to town, and they were hard to stop.
Print helped fuel the [[Renaissance]], the Reformation, and the Scientific Revolution, because ideas could finally be shared widely and checked by others.
Every book you read, every newspaper, even the pages on your screen carry a little of Gutenberg's legacy. One clever machine helped knowledge reach everyone.
